title: Klein Tunneling of Dirac Fermions through Electromagnetic Barriers
abstract: The Lorentz covariance of relativistic Dirac equations serves as a fundamental principle underlying the laws of electromagnetism across different inertial frames. Exploiting the covariance, we obtain the general solutions for Dirac fermions under both the in-plane electric $\boldsymbol{E}$ and perpendicular magnetic $\boldsymbol{B}$ fields, which reduce to either a magnetic or electric field in the inertial frame with drift velocity along the $\boldsymbol{E}\times\boldsymbol{B}$ direction. This dichotomy defines the magnetic and electric regimes, separated by the critical field ratio $E/B=v_\text{F}$ with $v_\text{F}$ denoting the Fermi velocity of Dirac fermions. Using these solutions, we revisit Klein tunneling through a heterojunction with generalized electromagnetic potentials. In the magnetic regime, the transmission exhibits oscillations governed by the Fabry-Pérot interference. In the electric regime, perfect transmission occurs at normal incidence in the drifted frame. The interference phase is further analyzed in terms of the solid angles on the Bloch sphere, providing a geometric interpretation of Klein tunneling. Finally, we briefly discuss the relation between the tilting of Dirac cones and the in-plane electric field, establishing the correspondence of the undertilted and overtilted cases to the magnetic and electric regimes, respectively. Our findings reveal the manipulation of Klein tunneling by electromagnetic fields, offering a theoretical basis for designing novel electronic devices.
summary: This theoretical work analyzes how Klein tunneling behaves for Dirac fermions traversing electromagnetic barriers. By exploiting Lorentz covariance, the authors derive solutions for different field regimes, showing that the transmission is controllable by the ratio of electric to magnetic fields. This offers a theoretical blueprint for engineering novel electronic devices based on field-controlled quantum transport.
main_problem: The paper investigates the phenomenon of Klein tunneling for Dirac fermions when passing through barriers subjected to generalized, spatially varying electromagnetic potentials.
main_result: The transmission of Dirac fermions through these barriers is highly dependent on the electromagnetic field configuration, exhibiting Fabry-Pérot oscillations in the magnetic regime and perfect transmission at normal incidence in the electric regime.
method: The analysis involves solving the manifestly covariant Dirac equation by exploiting Lorentz covariance to derive general solutions in different field regimes, followed by matching wave functions at the interfaces using transfer matrix formalism.
model_or_system: The system models Dirac fermions, relevant to topological insulators, propagating through a structure defined by bottom, side, and top surfaces, governed by the Dirac equation with electromagnetic potentials.
key_observables: Transmission probability (T), interference phase ($\Phi$), and the solid angles ($\Omega$) on the Bloch sphere.
important_parameters: The critical field ratio $E/B = v_F$ separates the magnetic and electric regimes; the drift velocity $v$ is a key parameter.
main_assumptions: Evanescent waves are neglected in the discussion of Klein tunneling, and the analysis relies on matching wave functions at the interfaces.
figures_summary: Figure 2 shows polar and line plots of transmission probability T in magnetic and electric regimes. Figure 3 displays the geometric phase on the Bloch sphere using solid angles $\Omega(\pm d)$.
paper_structure: The paper first derives general solutions by exploiting Lorentz covariance for Dirac fermions in $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ fields. It then applies these solutions to model Klein tunneling through a heterojunction, calculating transmission probability via transfer matrices and interpreting the phase geometrically.
why_interesting: The geometric interpretation of the interference phase using solid angles on the Bloch sphere provides a novel, visual framework for understanding quantum transport phenomena in relativistic electron systems.
